solution.concept_anchor: Article 132 tripartite coverage across all proceedings
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students associate 'constitutional questions' primarily with civil matters, making a civil-only restriction seem plausible.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options restricting Article 132 to civil proceedings — the article expressly mentions civil, criminal, AND other proceedings.
Eliminate options that require no certificate — a High Court certificate of fitness is a mandatory prerequisite under Article 132.
Eliminate options claiming Article 133 also covers criminal matters on constitutional grounds — Article 133 is strictly civil.
The correct answer is the option that captures both the tripartite scope and the certificate requirement under Article 132.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A student who has read Article 133 in isolation often assumes that constitutional questions in civil matters are covered there. The trap is conflating Articles 132 and 133. Article 132 is the only appellate provision that cuts across all three categories — civil, criminal, and other proceedings — on the sole basis of a substantial constitutional question. Examiners regularly test this by presenting a civil-only restriction on Article 132, which feels correct because Article 133 does deal with civil matters.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 132 grants the Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction over any judgment, decree, or order of a High Court — whether arising from civil, criminal, or other proceedings — provided a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution is involved. The HC must certify fitness for appeal.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Article 132 is not limited to civil proceedings; it covers criminal and other proceedings too.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Restricting Article 132 to civil and criminal (excluding 'other') proceedings is a partial-truth trap; the article's tripartite scope includes 'other proceedings' explicitly.
• Option (c): Incorrect — No valuation threshold exists under Article 132. A valuation criterion existed under the old Article 133 but was removed by the 30th Constitutional Amendment, 1972.
• Option (d): Correct — Article 132 covers civil, criminal, and other proceedings where a substantial constitutional question is involved and the HC certifies fitness.

Value Addition:
• Article 132 is unique in being the only appellate provision cutting across all three proceeding types on constitutional grounds.
• The HC certificate is mandatory — its refusal does not, however, bar an SLP under Article 136.
• A 'substantial question' means one not settled by existing precedent and materially affecting the parties' rights.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 133 dual threshold and 30th Amendment

statement_analysis.statement: Article 133 allows an appeal to the Supreme Court from any High Court judgment in a civil proceeding if the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance that needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: This captures the dual threshold under Article 133 — the question must be of 'general importance' AND the HC must certify that it 'needs to be decided' by the SC.

statement_analysis.statement: The 30th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1972 removed the requirement that the value of the subject matter in dispute must exceed a prescribed amount for invoking Article 133.
statement_analysis.reason: Before the 30th Amendment, a valuation criterion existed; the amendment deleted it, making the certificate-based route purely merit-driven.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 133 extends to criminal proceedings from High Courts in addition to civil proceedings.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 133 is exclusively confined to civil proceedings. Criminal appellate jurisdiction flows from Article 134.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 2 are both correct and well-known facts, tempting candidates to accept Statement 3 without scrutiny.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 3 — Article 133 is textually confined to civil proceedings; criminal jurisdiction is covered under Article 134, so Statement 3 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 1 — the dual threshold (general importance + needs to be decided) is the correct reading of Article 133, so Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2 — the 30th Constitutional Amendment, 1972 removed the valuation criterion, so Statement 2 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are correct, pointing to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Many candidates extend Article 133's reach to criminal matters by reasoning that constitutional questions in criminal proceedings should also attract a civil-appellate-type provision. The trap exploits the fact that Article 132 covers criminal proceedings on constitutional grounds, making students conflate the two articles. Statement 3 is the planted falsehood — Article 133 is strictly civil.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 133 governs civil appellate jurisdiction from High Courts to the Supreme Court. It imposes a dual threshold: (i) the question must be one of general importance, and (ii) the HC must certify that the question needs to be decided by the SC — both conditions must be satisfied.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The dual threshold is accurately stated. A certificate under Article 133 is not automatic; the HC must be satisfied on both limbs.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 30th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1972 removed the older valuation-based criterion, democratising access to SC appeals in civil matters.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 133 is restricted to civil proceedings. Criminal appellate jurisdiction from HCs is governed by Article 134, which has its own conditions including automatic jurisdiction in death-sentence cases.

Value Addition:
• Article 133(3) enables Parliament to confer additional appellate jurisdiction in civil matters by ordinary legislation.
• The 'needs to be decided' requirement means the HC must find the question unresolved by existing SC precedent.
• Even after HC refusal, a party may approach the SC directly via SLP under Article 136.

concepts_used: Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction under Article 134: Scope and Automatic vs. Certificate-Based Appeal

solution.concept_anchor: Article 134 automatic appeal — specific HC-order scenarios only

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 134, the Supreme Court automatically hears an appeal in every criminal case where the High Court has awarded the death sentence.
statement_analysis.reason: Automatic jurisdiction under Article 134(1)(a) and (b) arises only in two specific situations: when the HC reverses an acquittal and imposes death, or when the HC withdraws a case from a subordinate court and convicts with death. A mere death sentence by HC on first conviction does not trigger automatic SC jurisdiction.

statement_analysis.statement: The certificate-based route under Article 134(1)(c) requires the High Court to certify that the case is fit for appeal, which is the only pathway for a convicted person to appeal to the Supreme Court in criminal matters.
statement_analysis.reason: The certificate route under 134(1)(c) is one pathway, but it is NOT the only one. The automatic routes under 134(1)(a) and (b) are available without any certificate, and Parliament has also extended SC criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134(2) via the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 134 does not extend to appeals from courts other than High Courts — a person convicted by a Sessions Court must first obtain an HC judgment before invoking Article 134.
statement_analysis.reason: Articles 132–134 exclusively contemplate appeals from High Courts. A Sessions Court conviction must be taken to the HC first; Article 134 cannot be invoked bypassing the HC.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Statement 1 only is incorrect) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is the most visible error, and a partially prepared student may stop there without detecting the falsehood in Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1 — automatic SC jurisdiction under Article 134 does NOT attach to every HC death sentence; only reversal-of-acquittal and case-withdrawal-with-death scenarios qualify; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Examine Statement 2 — this claims the certificate route is the 'only' pathway, ignoring automatic jurisdiction and Parliament-extended jurisdiction; Statement 2 is also incorrect.
Examine Statement 3 — this is a correct statement; Articles 132–134 are strictly HC-to-SC tracks.
Both Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect, so the answer is option (c) — 1 and 2.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 1 exploits the widespread belief that any death sentence automatically reaches the Supreme Court. In reality, Article 134(1)(a) and (b) specify precise triggering conditions — HC reversal of acquittal leading to death, or HC withdrawing a lower-court case and imposing death. A straightforward HC confirmation of a death sentence does NOT create automatic SC jurisdiction. Statement 2's trap is the word 'only', which converts a true partial fact into a false absolute claim.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 134 provides criminal appellate jurisdiction to the Supreme Court through two channels: automatic (as of right) and certificate-based. The automatic route applies only when the HC reverses an acquittal and sentences the accused to death, or when the HC withdraws a case from a subordinate court and convicts with a death sentence. Any other criminal matter requires an HC certificate of fitness (134(1)(c)) or falls under Parliament-extended jurisdiction.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Not every HC death sentence creates automatic SC jurisdiction; only the two specific reversal/withdrawal scenarios under 134(1)(a)/(b) do.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The certificate route is one of multiple pathways — automatic jurisdiction and Parliament-enacted expansion (via the 1970 Act) also exist.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Articles 132–134 are exclusively HC-to-SC tracks; a Sessions Court judgment must first reach the HC.

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 was enacted under Article 134(2).
• Even after HC refuses a certificate under 134(1)(c), the accused may file an SLP under Article 136.
• Article 134A requires HCs to decide certificate applications promptly.

concepts_used: Parliamentary Power to Extend Appellate Jurisdiction under Articles 133(3) and 134(2)

solution.concept_anchor: Parliamentary expansion of SC appellate jurisdiction — ordinary law suffices

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament can expand the Supreme Court's criminal appellate jurisdiction by passing an ordinary law under Article 134(2).
statement_analysis.reason: Article 134(2) expressly empowers Parliament to confer further criminal appellate jurisdiction on the SC by ordinary legislation — no constitutional amendment is required.

statement_analysis.statement: The Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 was enacted using the power under Article 134(2) and requires a constitutional amendment to be modified.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1970 Act is ordinary legislation; it can be amended or repealed by Parliament through a simple majority — it is not entrenched as a constitutional provision.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliament's power to extend civil appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 133(3) is equivalent in legal character to the power under Article 134(2) — both require only an ordinary law.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Article 133(3) and Article 134(2) authorise Parliament to confer additional jurisdiction by ordinary legislation; neither requires a constitutional amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: Any law enacted by Parliament under Article 134(2) to extend criminal appellate jurisdiction of the SC amounts to an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliament-extended appellate jurisdiction under Article 134(2) flows through ordinary legislative power, not the special constituent power under Article 368. The Constitution itself permits this expansion via simple law.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (only two correct) is a strong distractor for students who mistakenly accept Statement 2 as correct, believing a law enacted under the Constitution requires constitutional-amendment procedures to amend.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is clearly correct — Article 134(2) expressly provides for parliamentary expansion by ordinary law.
Statement 2 contains the false claim that the 1970 Act requires a constitutional amendment to modify — it is ordinary legislation; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 is correct — both Art. 133(3) and Art. 134(2) operate through ordinary legislation.
Statement 4 is incorrect — ordinary law under Art. 134(2) is not an Art. 368 amendment; only Statements 1 and 3 are correct, pointing to option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the intuitive but incorrect assumption that a law which expands the jurisdiction of a constitutional court must itself be a constitutional amendment. Statements 2 and 4 both plant this false premise. In reality, Articles 133(3) and 134(2) explicitly authorise Parliament to expand SC appellate jurisdiction through ordinary legislation — a deliberate constitutional design to keep this flexible.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 133(3) and 134(2) represent a unique constitutional design: they allow Parliament to expand the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction — civil and criminal respectively — through ordinary legislation, without touching Article 368. This is a legislative, not constituent, exercise of power.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 134(2) explicitly provides this power via ordinary law.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 1970 Act is ordinary legislation; a simple parliamentary majority can amend or repeal it.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Both Art. 133(3) and Art. 134(2) are ordinary-law tracks for expansion.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Legislation under Art. 134(2) is not an Art. 368 constitutional amendment.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (a).

Value Addition:
• The Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 lowered the threshold for criminal appeals, bringing more cases within SC reach.
• This design contrasts with amendment of Art. 124 (SC judges) which requires a special majority.
• Parliament's power here is enabling, not self-executing — SC does not automatically get expanded jurisdiction; a specific law must be enacted.

solution.concept_anchor: HC certificate routes under Arts. 132/133/134 vs. SLP under Art. 136
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because it correctly places Art. 136 as 'filed before SC' but mismatches the certificate articles, exploiting candidates' uncertainty about which article covers which proceeding type.
elimination_logic: Article 132 covers constitutional questions in all proceedings (civil/criminal/other) — it pairs with 'Substantial question of constitutional interpretation; covers civil, criminal, and other proceedings'.
Article 133 is strictly civil — it pairs with 'Confined to civil proceedings; dual threshold of general importance and needs to be decided'.
Article 134 is criminal with automatic routes — it pairs with 'Includes automatic appeal route for specific death-sentence scenarios'.
Article 136 is the SLP filed directly before the SC, not through an HC certificate — it pairs with 'Discretionary jurisdiction; petition filed directly before the Supreme Court'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in pairing Articles 133 and 134. Candidates who know both articles deal with HC-to-SC appeals sometimes reverse their attributes, placing criminal jurisdiction under Art. 133 or civil under Art. 134. The automatic appeal route in Art. 134 is the precise differentiator. Similarly, confusing HC-certificate-based routes with Art. 136 SLP (which is filed before the SC directly) is a classic conflation error.
solution.final_explanation:
The SC's appellate jurisdiction operates through distinct channels depending on the nature of the proceedings and the mechanism for invoking jurisdiction.

Correct matches:
• A-3: Article 132 covers constitutional questions across civil, criminal, and other proceedings — the only tripartite provision.
• B-4: Article 133 is exclusively civil, with a dual threshold — the question must be of general importance AND the HC must certify it needs SC resolution.
• C-1: Article 134 is criminal, uniquely including automatic appeal routes when HC reverses acquittal and sentences to death.
• D-2: Article 136 SLP is filed directly before the SC — it is not HC-certificate-based but a discretionary grant-of-leave mechanism.

Trap pairing: C and B are frequently swapped by candidates who confuse civil/criminal coverage.

Value Addition:
• HC refusal of certificate under Arts. 132/133/134 does not extinguish the party's right to seek SLP under Art. 136.
• Art. 136 is broader — it reaches courts AND tribunals; Arts. 132–134 reach only HCs.
• The SC can examine the correctness of an HC certificate even after it is granted.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 136 discretionary leave — not appellate jurisdiction per se
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and students instinctively assume the reason explains the assertion without checking whether the causal link holds.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) factually correct? A states that SC can refuse an SLP without assigning reasons — Yes, this is correct; Art. 136 is a discretionary power.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) factually correct? R states that military tribunals/courts-martial are excluded from Art. 136 — Yes, this is correct under Art. 136(2).

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? R explains a specific exclusion under Art. 136(2), but the SC's power to refuse SLP without reasons flows from the general discretionary nature of Art. 136(1), not from the military exclusion in Art. 136(2). R does NOT explain A.
A is correct, R is correct, but R does not explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are independently verifiable facts drawn from Article 136. The trap is that they appear thematically connected — both are about Art. 136 — making the causal link seem automatic. However, the SC's discretion to refuse SLPs without reasons is a feature of Art. 136(1)'s grant of extraordinary jurisdiction; the military exclusion in Art. 136(2) is a separate, distinct feature. One does not cause or explain the other.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 136 grants the Supreme Court discretionary and extraordinary power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment of any court or tribunal in India.

Assertion (A): Correct — The SC may grant or refuse leave under Art. 136 without assigning reasons; this is inherent in the word 'discretion' in the article.

Reason (R): Correct — Article 136(2) specifically excludes courts-martial and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces from Art. 136 jurisdiction.

Causal relationship: R describes a jurisdictional exclusion — a carve-out for military adjudication. The SC's liberty to refuse SLPs without reasons flows from the plenary discretionary character of Art. 136(1), which exists independently of the military exclusion. The exclusion in Art. 136(2) does not cause or justify the no-reasons rule; that rule applies across all non-excluded matters. R, though factually correct, does not explain A.

Value Addition:
• Art. 136 is often called the 'residual appellate jurisdiction' — a safety valve for extraordinary situations.
• The Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007 provides an internal appellate mechanism for military matters.
• SC has consistently held that Art. 136 is not an ordinary right of appeal but a special discretionary power.

solution.concept_anchor: Sequence: appellate judgment → review → curative petition
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c reverses the position of the review petition and the curative petition, exploiting candidates who know both exist but are uncertain which comes first.
elimination_logic: A curative petition is a remedy AFTER the review petition is dismissed — so 'dismissal of review petition' must precede 'filing of curative petition'.
An appellate judgment by the SC must precede both review and curative proceedings — it is the subject-matter of subsequent remedies.

The Rupa Ashok Hurra case (2002) which evolved the curative petition came after the constitutional review mechanism under Art. 137 was already in operation — confirming the appellate judgment → review → curative sequence.
Correct sequence: SC appellate judgment → review petition under Art. 137 → curative petition post-review dismissal — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Candidates who know about curative petitions sometimes believe they run parallel to review petitions rather than being a subsequent remedy. The 2002 Rupa Ashok Hurra judgment is clear: a curative petition lies only after the review petition has been dismissed. Placing the curative petition before review (or equating them as simultaneous remedies) is the classic temporal-swap error.
solution.final_explanation:
Post-judgment remedies in the Supreme Court follow a strict sequence. Once the SC delivers an appellate judgment, a review petition may be filed under Article 137. This is the first post-judgment internal remedy. Only after the SC dismisses the review petition does a curative petition — a judicially evolved remedy from Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002) — become maintainable.

Correct sequence — Event I → Event II → Event III:
1. SC delivers its appellate judgment
2. Aggrieved party files a review petition under Article 137
3. After review is dismissed, a curative petition is filed

Why wrong options fail:
• Options placing curative before review violate the sequential logic — curative is expressly available only post-review dismissal.
• Options suggesting review and curative can be filed simultaneously misread the Hurra judgment.

Value Addition:
• Art. 137 review is typically decided in chambers without oral arguments; curative petitions are heard by the three senior-most judges plus the bench that decided the original case.
• Grounds for review include error apparent on the face of the record and new evidence.
• Curative petitions are extremely rare — SC emphasises finality of judgments as a core value.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 32 writ vs. Art. 136 SLP — distinct jurisdictions, no substitution
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because it correctly describes Article 32 as an original jurisdiction but erroneously suggests it can serve as a substitute for an available appellate remedy, which the SC has consistently rejected.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a party challenging an HC decision — this is quintessentially the domain of Art. 136 SLP, not Art. 32.
Art. 32 requires a distinct and independent violation of fundamental rights — it cannot be used merely to route around an available appellate remedy.
SC has held that when an effective appellate remedy under Art. 136 exists, Art. 32 should not be invoked as a substitute.
The correct principle is that Art. 32 and Art. 136 are parallel tracks — but Art. 32 requires an independent FRs basis, not just dissatisfaction with an HC ruling; option (d) captures this.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the widespread understanding that Article 32 is a fundamental right that cannot be abridged. Students may reason that since Art. 32 is a fundamental right itself, it can be invoked in any situation. However, the SC has consistently held that Art. 32 is not a substitute for an appeal — it requires an independent and distinct FRs violation. Treating HC's wrong decision as itself an FRs violation to trigger Art. 32 is the conflation that examiners test.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 32 confers original jurisdiction on the SC for enforcement of fundamental rights. Article 136 confers discretionary appellate jurisdiction via SLP. These are distinct channels with distinct purposes.

Applicable principle: The SC has held that Article 32 cannot be used as a substitute for an appeal when an effective appellate remedy exists. A party dissatisfied with an HC ruling must use Article 136 (SLP). Article 32 requires a fresh, independent violation of fundamental rights — not merely an error by the HC.

Mapping to the scenario: Amara's HC decision is an error of law, not an independent violation of a fundamental right. The correct route is an SLP under Art. 136.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Art. 131 is for inter-governmental disputes, not private party-state HC litigation.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Art. 32 is original jurisdiction for FRs enforcement; it cannot substitute for an available appellate remedy.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Art. 143 is the advisory jurisdiction; it applies to Presidential references, not party litigation.
• Option (d): Correct — The SC has consistently held that Art. 32 and Art. 136 are parallel but not interchangeable; Art. 32 requires an independent FRs basis.

Value Addition:
• Art. 32 itself is a fundamental right under Part III — it cannot be suspended except during a national emergency.
• SC has issued guidelines discouraging Art. 32 petitions when High Court remedies remain unutilised.
• Art. 226 (HC writ) and Art. 32 (SC writ) serve similar purposes but at different court levels.

solution.concept_anchor: L. Chandra Kumar — HC jurisdiction over tribunals mandatory before SC
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (National Green Tribunal) is a strong distractor because it is a specialised tribunal with its own appellate structure, leading candidates to assume it might be excluded from HC scrutiny like military tribunals.
elimination_logic: The L. Chandra Kumar case (1997) held that tribunal orders must be subject to HC scrutiny (under Arts. 226/227) before reaching the SC — this applies to CAT, NGT, and NCLT.
Military courts-martial are expressly excluded from Art. 136 jurisdiction under Art. 136(2) — this is a constitutional exclusion, not a Chandra Kumar exclusion.
CAT, NGT, and NCLT are all civil/administrative/economic tribunals subject to HC supervisory jurisdiction before SC.
Courts-martial do not go through HC under Arts. 226/227 — they are the odd one out in this group.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is that NGT has a specialised appellate structure, making it look like it might share the military tribunal's exclusion from Art. 136. However, the military courts-martial exclusion is a specific constitutional carve-out under Art. 136(2). NGT, CAT, and NCLT orders all go through HC under Arts. 226/227 before reaching the SC via Art. 136 — exactly as mandated by the L. Chandra Kumar principle.
solution.final_explanation:
The L. Chandra Kumar case (1997) established that judicial review by HCs (under Arts. 226/227) is a basic structure feature — tribunal orders must pass through HC scrutiny before reaching the SC. This applies to the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), National Green Tribunal (NGT), and National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).

• CAT: Administrative tribunal; HC has supervisory jurisdiction under Art. 226/227.
• NGT: Environmental tribunal; HC jurisdiction as intermediate appellate forum.
• NCLT: Company law tribunal; HC jurisdiction applies before SC under Art. 136.
• Courts-martial: Constitutionally excluded from Art. 136 by Art. 136(2); military discipline is governed by Army/Navy/Air Force Acts with a separate framework — no HC or SC appellate route.

Courts-martial do NOT belong to the same group as the others, which are all tribunals subject to HC and then SC jurisdiction.

Value Addition:
• Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank (2019) reaffirmed Chandra Kumar — SC cannot be the first appellate court over tribunals.
• Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007 provides internal review for military matters.
• Art. 136(2) exclusion is precise — it covers only Armed Forces-related tribunals/courts-martial.

concepts_used: 'Substantial Question of Law' as a Threshold Concept across Articles 132 and 133

solution.concept_anchor: Substantial question — constitutional vs. general importance qualifier

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 132, the substantial question of law must be one relating specifically to the interpretation of the Constitution, whereas under Article 133, the substantial question must be of general importance — not confined to constitutional interpretation.
statement_analysis.reason: This captures the precise qualifier difference: Art. 132 requires a 'constitutional' question while Art. 133 requires one of 'general importance' — broader in scope but not limited to the Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: A question already settled by a binding Supreme Court precedent can still qualify as a 'substantial question of law' under Articles 132 and 133 if it affects a large number of people.
statement_analysis.reason: Judicial interpretation consistently holds that a 'substantial question' is one NOT covered by settled law. If the question is settled by SC precedent, it is no longer 'substantial' — the number of people affected does not override the settled-law disqualification.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is accurate and well-reasoned, pulling candidates toward assuming Statement 2 is also correct on the basis of a commonsense reading of 'general importance'.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Art. 132 uses 'constitutional interpretation' and Art. 133 uses 'general importance'; these are distinct qualifiers correctly stated; Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 2 — judicial interpretation requires that a substantial question be one NOT settled by existing precedent; large-scale impact does not revive a settled question; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct and Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the intuitive appeal of 'affecting many people' as a marker of importance. Candidates who conflate 'general importance' with 'widespread impact' will accept Statement 2. However, the legal threshold for 'substantial question' requires the absence of settled law — large-scale impact does not create a new substantial question if the law is already clear.
solution.final_explanation:
The phrase 'substantial question of law' appears in both Articles 132 and 133 but with different qualifiers that are frequently tested.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 132 confines the threshold to constitutional interpretation; Art. 133 broadens it to any question of general importance, which could include statutory interpretation or common law principles — not just constitutional ones.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: A settled question of law cannot be 'substantial' regardless of how many people are affected. The test is whether the question is open, unresolved, or conflicts with prior rulings — not the scale of its impact.

Value Addition:
• A question of law is 'substantial' if it is debatable, not obviously concluded, and materially affects the parties' legal rights.
• Under Art. 133, the HC must also certify the question 'needs to be decided' by the SC — a second separate threshold.
• Under Art. 132, once a constitutional question exists, all three proceeding types (civil/criminal/other) are covered.

Review Jurisdiction under Article 137 as a Complement to Appellate Jurisdiction

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 137 review jurisdiction — separate from appellate jurisdiction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Article 136) is a strong distractor because students associate SC's power to revisit decisions most readily with the SLP power, not realising that Art. 136 is for reviewing lower court orders, not SC's own judgments.
elimination_logic: The blank asks for the provision under which SC reviews its OWN judgments — Art. 136 is for appeals from lower courts, so eliminate option (a).
Art. 131 is original jurisdiction for government disputes — eliminate option (c).
Art. 142 is the complete-justice power during proceedings — it does not govern self-review; eliminate option (d).
Art. 137 specifically empowers SC to review any judgment or order made by itself — option (b) is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Candidates who know Art. 136 as the broad SLP power sometimes confuse it with the SC's power to revisit its own decisions. Art. 136 is an appellate jurisdiction over lower courts and tribunals. The SC's self-review power derives from Art. 137 — a distinct and narrower provision governed by SC rules under Art. 145.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court has multiple post-judgment powers that must be carefully distinguished.

• Option (a) — Article 136: Incorrect. Art. 136 grants discretionary leave to appeal from lower courts and tribunals — it does not empower the SC to review its own prior judgments.
• Option (b) — Article 137: Correct. Art. 137 empowers the SC to review any judgment or order made by it, subject to laws made by Parliament and rules framed under Art. 145.
• Option (c) — Article 131: Incorrect. Art. 131 is original jurisdiction for disputes between States or between States and the Centre — unrelated to self-review.
• Option (d) — Article 142: Incorrect. Art. 142 is the power to pass any order necessary for complete justice during pending proceedings — not a review mechanism.

Value Addition:
• Review petitions under Art. 137 are typically heard in chambers (without oral arguments) by the same bench that delivered the original judgment.
• Grounds for review include error apparent on the face of the record, discovery of new and important matter, or any other sufficient reason.
• A curative petition (post-Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002) lies only after the review petition itself has been dismissed.

concepts_used: Curative Petition: Judicial Evolution Beyond Constitutional Text

solution.concept_anchor: Curative petition — Rupa Ashok Hurra 2002 origin and bench composition
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is a strong distractor because it places the curative petition under Art. 137, which is the real review jurisdiction provision, making the conflation with review seem authoritative.
elimination_logic: The curative petition was evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), not under any constitutional article — eliminate options attributing it to a constitutional provision.
The curative bench consists of the three senior-most judges plus the judges who delivered the original judgment — options stating a different composition are incorrect.
Option (a) correctly identifies both the case origin (2002, Rupa Ashok Hurra) and the key ground (natural justice/bias) — this is the correctly matched pair.
Options (b), (c), (d) each contain a fabricated or swapped element — wrong case, wrong article, or wrong ground.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) pairs the curative petition with Article 137, which is plausible because both deal with post-judgment SC remedies. However, Art. 137 is the constitutionally enumerated review power; the curative petition is entirely judge-made law from the 2002 Hurra decision. Examiners test this distinction precisely because both are 'post-review-of-SC-judgment' remedies, yet one is constitutional text and the other is judicial evolution.
solution.final_explanation:
The curative petition is a judicially evolved remedy with no textual basis in the Constitution.

• Option (a): Correct — The curative petition was evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002). Grounds include violation of natural justice principles or a judge's apprehension of bias. The bench comprises three senior-most judges plus the judges who passed the original judgment.
• Option (b): Incorrect — The 2002 judgment's parties are Rupa Ashok Hurra, not 'Antulay' — a plausible-fabrication trap using a real but unrelated case name.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Curative petition is not a constitutional provision under Art. 137; Art. 137 is the statutory review power. Attributing the curative petition to Art. 137 conflates two distinct remedies.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Grounds for curative petition are natural justice violations and bias, not discovery of new evidence (which is a ground for Art. 137 review).

Value Addition:
• Curative petitions are extremely rare and almost never granted; finality of judgment is the SC's default posture.
• The curative petition concept draws from the maxim: actus curiae neminem gravabit (an act of the court shall prejudice no one).
• Unlike review, curative petitions may involve a brief oral hearing.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 139A — 44th Amendment, transfer vs. appellate jurisdiction

statement_analysis.statement: Article 139A empowers the Supreme Court to transfer cases involving the same or substantially similar questions of law pending before two or more High Courts, or between a High Court and the Supreme Court itself, to a single court for a consolidated ruling.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 139A explicitly permits SC to transfer such cases to itself or any other HC for uniform adjudication — consolidation for consistency is the core purpose.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 139A was part of the original Constitution as adopted in 1950, recognising early the need for the Supreme Court to prevent conflicting rulings across High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 139A was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 — it is not an original provision of the Constitution.

statement_analysis.statement: Transfer under Article 139A is fundamentally different from appellate jurisdiction — transfer consolidates pending cases before a judgment is given, whereas appellate jurisdiction is invoked after a lower court has delivered its decision.
statement_analysis.reason: This distinction is accurate and conceptually important: Art. 139A operates on pending matters to prevent inconsistent outcomes, while Arts. 132–134/136 operate post-decision.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Statements 1 and 2) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is correct, and a student unfamiliar with the 44th Amendment insertion may accept Statement 2 as a plausible original provision.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 2 — Art. 139A was inserted by the 44th Amendment, 1978, not in the original 1950 Constitution; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 1 — the description of Art. 139A's transfer power is accurate; Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 3 — the distinction between transfer (pre-judgment, pending cases) and appellate jurisdiction (post-judgment review) is precisely correct; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the tendency of candidates to assume that core judicial provisions are original. The 44th Amendment (1978) inserted Art. 139A during a period of significant constitutional changes following the Emergency. Candidates who know the 44th Amendment primarily for the restoration of 'liberty' in Art. 21 may not recall its judicial provisions. The year '1950' in Statement 2 is the temporal-swap trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 139A was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 — a significant post-Emergency reform. It empowers the SC to transfer cases involving substantially similar questions of law from one HC to another, or from an HC to the SC, to ensure uniform rulings.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 139A permits the SC to consolidate pending matters across courts; parties can also apply for transfer.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Art. 139A is not original — it was added in 1978 via the 44th Amendment. The original Constitution did not contain this provision.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Transfer under Art. 139A is prospective and pre-judgment; appellate jurisdiction is retrospective and post-judgment.

Value Addition:
• The 44th Amendment, 1978 also restored 'life and personal liberty' protections weakened during the Emergency and inserted Art. 20/21 protections.
• Art. 139A can be invoked suo motu by the SC or on the application of a party.
• Art. 139A is distinct from Art. 136 SLP — it does not require a lower court decision to have been made.

High Court as the Feeder Court for SC Appellate Jurisdiction: Role of Articles 132–134

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 136 covers interlocutory orders; Arts. 132–134 limited to final HC orders

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court's jurisdiction is restricted to final judgments of courts and tribunals — interlocutory orders cannot be challenged through a Special Leave Petition.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 136's text covers 'any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order' — the word 'order' includes interlocutory orders. SC has consistently held that interim orders causing irreversible harm are challengeable via SLP.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Articles 132, 133, and 134, the Supreme Court can be approached directly from a Sessions Court or District Court judgment without first obtaining a High Court ruling, provided a constitutional question is involved.
statement_analysis.reason: Arts. 132–134 expressly refer to judgments, decrees, or orders of High Courts — they cannot be invoked bypassing the HC. A Sessions or District Court ruling must reach the HC before these articles apply.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 136 applies to courts and tribunals throughout the territory of India, thereby providing a wider ambit than Articles 132, 133, and 134 which are confined to High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 136 explicitly covers any court or tribunal (except military); Arts. 132–134 are limited to HC-to-SC tracks. This comparative scope difference is accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Statement 2 only is incorrect) is a strong distractor because Statement 2's error is obvious and candidates may stop there, missing that Statement 1 is also incorrect.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1 — Art. 136 uses the word 'order' which covers interlocutory orders; SC has allowed SLPs against interim orders causing irreversible harm; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Test Statement 2 — Arts. 132–134 explicitly require a High Court judgment; bypassing HC is not possible under these articles; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Test Statement 3 — Art. 136's broader coverage vs. Arts. 132–134's HC-only scope is correctly described; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are both incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is the principal trap: the instinct that only final judgments can be challenged at the SC level causes candidates to accept it as true. However, Art. 136's text is deliberately broad — 'any…order' — and SC has repeatedly entertained SLPs against interlocutory orders when irreversible harm would result from waiting for the final judgment. Statement 2 exploits unfamiliarity with the HC-feeder-court requirement.
solution.final_explanation:
Articles 132–134 and Article 136 differ significantly in textual coverage and the stage at which they can be invoked.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Art. 136 covers 'any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order' — the term 'order' is wide enough to include interlocutory orders. SC has accepted SLPs against interim orders in cases of irreversible harm.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Arts. 132–134 are strictly HC-to-SC appellate tracks. There is no direct path from a Sessions/District Court to the SC under these articles; HC must adjudicate first.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Art. 136's coverage of any court or tribunal (minus military) makes it broader than Arts. 132–134, which are limited to HC orders.

Value Addition:
• Art. 136's broad 'order' language was intentional — the framers wanted a safety valve for extraordinary situations at any stage of proceedings.
• Even under Art. 136, SC exercises extreme caution before interfering with interlocutory orders to avoid disrupting ongoing proceedings.
• Arts. 132–134 represent the structured, hierarchical appeal route; Art. 136 is the extraordinary bypass.

solution.concept_anchor: Automatic appeal as of right — precise triggering conditions under Art. 134

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court reverses an acquittal by a subordinate court and sentences the accused to death — the accused has an automatic right of appeal to the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: This precisely matches Article 134(1)(a): HC reversal of acquittal with death sentence gives an automatic right of appeal without requiring any certificate.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court confirms a death sentence originally awarded by a Sessions Court — the accused has an automatic right of appeal to the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 134(1)(a)/(b) require either reversal of acquittal to death or withdrawal of a case from subordinate court followed by death sentence. Mere confirmation of a Sessions Court death sentence does not trigger automatic SC jurisdiction.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court withdraws a case from a subordinate court and in the trial concludes with a conviction and death sentence — an automatic right of appeal to the SC is triggered.
statement_analysis.reason: This matches Art. 134(1)(b): HC's withdrawal of a case and subsequent conviction with death sentence creates an automatic right of appeal.

statement_analysis.statement: A High Court, exercising its appellate jurisdiction, reduces a death sentence to life imprisonment — the state government has an automatic right of appeal to the Supreme Court against the reduction.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 134(1)(a)/(b) do not provide for automatic appeals by the State against commutation. The automatic right of appeal under Art. 134 is specifically triggered by the two defined scenarios, neither of which covers a state's challenge to sentence reduction.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (only two correct) is a strong distractor for students who confuse pair 2 (confirmation of death sentence) with the automatic right scenario, accepting it because it also involves a death sentence.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 matches Art. 134(1)(a) precisely — correct.
Statement 2 involves HC confirming (not reversing) a lower court death sentence — this does not trigger Art. 134(1)(a)/(b); incorrect.
Statement 3 matches Art. 134(1)(b) — HC withdraws the case and convicts with death; correct.
Statement 4 involves a state appealing against commutation — no automatic right exists for this; incorrect. Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statements 2 and 4 both involve death sentence scenarios, and candidates who reason from the general principle 'death sentences reach SC automatically' will mark them correct. The trap is the UPSC-favourite distinction: only reversal of acquittal and HC-withdrawal-followed-by-death trigger automatic jurisdiction. Death sentences generally — confirmation, original sentencing, or commutation challenges — do not.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 134(1)(a) and (b) identify exactly two scenarios where appeal to the SC is a matter of right (no certificate needed):
(a) HC reverses acquittal and sentences to death.
(b) HC withdraws a case from subordinate court and concludes with conviction and death sentence.

• Statement 1 — Correct: HC reversal of acquittal + death sentence = automatic appeal under 134(1)(a).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: HC confirmation of a Sessions Court death sentence does NOT trigger automatic SC jurisdiction — the automatic route requires reversal or withdrawal.
• Statement 3 — Correct: HC withdrawal of case + conviction + death sentence = automatic appeal under 134(1)(b).
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: No automatic right exists for the State to appeal against commutation; this would require an HC certificate under 134(1)(c) or an SLP under Art. 136.

Only two statements are correct — option (b).

Value Addition:
• Art. 134A requires HCs to decide certificate applications expeditiously.
• Parliament expanded criminal appellate jurisdiction further via the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 under Art. 134(2).
• The automatic right is a constitutional guarantee for those facing the irreversible consequence of capital punishment in specific HC-originating scenarios.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 141 — 'all courts' excludes SC itself; ratio vs. obiter
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and the causal link between a single-judge bench decision binding HCs and the Art. 141 'all courts' mandate seems intuitive — students may not probe whether R actually explains the single-bench binding power.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that even a single-judge SC bench decision binds all High Courts — Yes, Art. 141 says 'law declared by SC' is binding on 'all courts' without any bench-strength exception; A is correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? R states that Art. 141's 'all courts' does not include the SC itself — Yes, this is correct; SC can depart from its own precedent via a larger bench; R is correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? A is about single-bench binding power over HCs; R explains that SC is excluded from 'all courts' — R explains the LIMIT of Art. 141 (SC not bound by its own precedents) but does NOT explain WHY a single-judge bench binds HCs. The reason for A is simply that Art. 141 applies to 'all courts' without a numerical strength qualifier, not the exclusion of SC itself.
A correct + R correct + R does not explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap: both A and R are independently correct facts about Art. 141, and they are closely related thematically — both deal with who is and isn't bound by SC precedents. This makes the causal link feel natural. However, the specific fact in A (single-judge bench binding HCs) is explained by the absence of a bench-strength qualifier in Art. 141, not by the fact that the SC itself is outside 'all courts'. R explains SC's freedom from its own precedents — a different aspect of Art. 141.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 141 declares that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.

Assertion (A): Correct — Art. 141 uses the phrase 'all courts' without any qualification based on bench strength. Therefore, a decision of even a single-judge SC bench constitutes 'law declared by SC' and binds all High Courts and subordinate courts. (Though conventionally significant questions are referred to larger benches.)

Reason (R): Correct — Art. 141's phrase 'all courts' has been judicially interpreted to exclude the Supreme Court itself. The SC can depart from its earlier decisions through a larger constitutional bench — it is not bound by its own precedent in the way HCs are.

Causal link: R correctly states that SC is not within 'all courts'. However, this fact explains SC's freedom to overrule its own decisions — it does NOT explain why a single-judge SC bench binds HCs. That binding force flows from the absence of any bench-strength condition in Art. 141. R is a true but causally unconnected explanation for A.

Value Addition:
• Only ratio decidendi (binding reason for the decision) is binding under Art. 141 — obiter dicta (incidental remarks) are persuasive, not binding.
• A larger bench can overrule a smaller bench's decision; this is the SC's internal hierarchy of precedent.
• Art. 141 creates vertical stare decisis — SC decisions bind courts below, but SC retains horizontal flexibility.

concepts_used: Scope of SC's Power to Pass Any Order in Appellate Jurisdiction under Article 142

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 142 — supplementary to appellate jurisdiction, not itself appellate
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because Art. 142 is most frequently exercised during appellate proceedings, leading students to conflate it with appellate jurisdiction itself.
elimination_logic: Eliminate options describing Art. 142 as a self-contained appellate jurisdiction — it does not grant the SC the power to hear appeals; that comes from Arts. 132–134/136.
Art. 142 is invoked while the SC is already exercising some other jurisdiction (original, appellate, advisory) — it is a power to mould relief, not a gateway jurisdiction.

Eliminate options claiming Art. 142 can override substantive statutory law — the Union Carbide controversy is unsettled, but the dominant view is that Art. 142 cannot be used to override clear statutory provisions.
The correct characterisation is that Art. 142 is a supplementary/ancillary power that enhances the SC's ability to do complete justice within its existing jurisdiction — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Candidates who regularly read SC judgments see Art. 142 invoked in appellate proceedings and begin treating it as part of appellate jurisdiction. The trap is the conflation — Art. 142 is an enabling/supplementary power that can be used in any jurisdiction the SC is exercising. It does not grant the SC the power to hear any new matter; it only expands the relief-moulding capacity within an already-vested jurisdiction.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or make any order necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it.

• Option (a): Incorrect — Art. 142 does not independently constitute appellate jurisdiction. It is a supplementary power operative only while SC is exercising some other jurisdiction.
• Option (b): Correct — Art. 142 is an ancillary/supplementary power that allows the SC to fashion remedies beyond what parties specifically prayed for, but always within the context of a matter already before the court.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Art. 142 does not empower SC to override clear statutory provisions; the Union Carbide controversy aside, the dominant judicial view is that Art. 142 fills procedural and remedial gaps but cannot abrogate substantive law.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Art. 142 applies in any matter before the SC — original, appellate, or advisory — not exclusively in appellate proceedings.

Value Addition:
• Art. 142 has been used in high-profile cases: Bhopal Gas settlement review, construction of Taj Trapezium regulations, dissolution of marriages in 'irretrievable breakdown' cases.
• The provision is unique globally — few constitutions grant courts such broad remedial latitude.
• Critics argue Art. 142 has sometimes been used to override legislative policy, blurring separation of powers.

solution.concept_anchor: L. Chandra Kumar 1997 — HC scrutiny of tribunals is basic structure

statement_analysis.statement: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that judicial review exercised by the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 over tribunal orders constitutes a basic feature of the Constitution and cannot be excluded by Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: L. Chandra Kumar unequivocally held that HC's power of judicial review over tribunals is part of the basic structure; Parliament cannot exclude it through ordinary legislation or even a constitutional amendment that damages this core.

statement_analysis.statement: The Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2019) judgment departed from the L. Chandra Kumar ruling by permitting direct appeals from certain tribunals to the Supreme Court without an intermediate High Court hearing.
statement_analysis.reason: Rojer Mathew (2019) reaffirmed L. Chandra Kumar — it upheld the need for HC jurisdiction as an intermediate appellate forum and did not create any exception permitting bypassing of HC scrutiny.

statement_analysis.statement: Even if Parliament enacts a law making the Supreme Court the first appellate court for tribunal orders (bypassing High Courts), such a law would be constitutionally invalid in light of the L. Chandra Kumar ruling.
statement_analysis.reason: L. Chandra Kumar held that bypassing HC review of tribunals violates the basic structure of judicial review; a law creating direct SC access over tribunal orders while excluding HC would be unconstitutional.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is a strong distractor because students who know L. Chandra Kumar may assume Rojer Mathew also endorsed the same direction without noting that Statement 2 claims a 'departure' — which is false.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 accurately describes L. Chandra Kumar (1997) — HC judicial review over tribunals = basic structure; Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2 falsely claims Rojer Mathew 'departed' from Chandra Kumar; Rojer Mathew reaffirmed it; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 follows logically from L. Chandra Kumar's basic structure ruling — Parliament cannot validly bypass HC scrutiny; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap is subtle: it uses a real and recent case (Rojer Mathew, 2019) that is thematically related to L. Chandra Kumar, but falsely attributes a 'departure' to it. Candidates who have heard of Rojer Mathew but have not studied it carefully may accept the departure claim, assuming the 2019 judgment evolved the law differently. In reality, it reinforced the Chandra Kumar principle.
solution.final_explanation:
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) is a landmark judgment on the constitutional relationship between tribunals, High Courts, and the Supreme Court.

• Statement 1 — Correct: HC judicial review (Arts. 226/227) over tribunal orders is a basic structure feature — Parliament cannot exclude it by any legislation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd. (2019) did NOT depart from Chandra Kumar. The Constitution Bench reaffirmed that HC jurisdiction must be available as an intermediate appellate forum before matters reach the SC via Art. 136.
• Statement 3 — Correct: A law making SC the first appellate court for tribunal orders (bypassing HC) would violate the basic structure as identified in Chandra Kumar and would be struck down.

Value Addition:
• Chandra Kumar overruled S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) which had held that adequate judicial review before tribunals could substitute for HC review.
• Rojer Mathew additionally referred certain questions about tribunal composition to a larger bench.
• This jurisprudence reflects the tension between Parliament's power to create tribunals (Art. 323A/323B) and the judicial review guarantee of the Constitution.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 136(2) military exclusion — precise constitutional carve-out

statement_analysis.statement: Article 136(2) excludes all specialised tribunals — including the Central Administrative Tribunal, National Green Tribunal, and courts-martial — from the Special Leave Petition jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 136(2) exclusively excludes courts-martial and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces. CAT and NGT are NOT excluded — they fall under Art. 136's general jurisdiction.

statement_analysis.statement: The rationale for excluding courts-martial from Article 136 jurisdiction is the existence of a separate judicial framework for the Armed Forces under the Army Act, Navy Act, and Air Force Act, which maintains military discipline through an independent adjudicatory structure.
statement_analysis.reason: This correctly identifies the constitutional rationale — military discipline and the separate legislative framework for Armed Forces justify the carve-out in Art. 136(2).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a (both correct) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is clearly correct and sounds authoritative; candidates may accept Statement 1 by over-generalising from the military exclusion to all specialised tribunals.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1 — Art. 136(2) lists only 'courts-martial or tribunals constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces'; CAT and NGT are not Armed Forces tribunals; Statement 1's inclusion of CAT/NGT is an entity-swap error; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 2 — the rationale of separate military judicial framework (Army Act, Navy Act, Air Force Act) is the correct reason for the Art. 136(2) exclusion; Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1's trap is the entity-swap: pulling CAT and NGT into the military exclusion. Candidates who know Art. 136(2) creates an exclusion but are fuzzy about its precise scope may accept a broadened version of it. The exclusion is narrow and specific — only Armed Forces-related courts and tribunals. CAT is an administrative tribunal and NGT is an environmental tribunal; neither is Armed Forces-related.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 136(2) creates a specific and narrow exclusion from the SC's SLP jurisdiction.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Art. 136(2) excludes ONLY courts-martial and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces. CAT, NGT, and other specialised tribunals are NOT excluded — they fall within Art. 136's general jurisdiction and their orders must go through HC (Arts. 226/227) before reaching the SC.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The rationale for the exclusion is the existence of a comprehensive, separate judicial framework for the military — the Army Act (1950), Navy Act (1957), and Air Force Act (1950) — which provides internal review mechanisms consistent with military discipline requirements.

Value Addition:
• The Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007 created a dedicated appellate body for service-related disputes, with its own internal review mechanism.
• Art. 136(2) is a rare instance of the Constitution directly excluding an entire category from SC jurisdiction — demonstrating the framers' deference to military autonomy.
• Despite the Art. 136(2) exclusion, writ jurisdiction under Art. 32 may still be available for fundamental rights violations in military contexts — though courts exercise caution.

solution.concept_anchor: Jurisdictional demarcation — Art. 131/132/143/129/32
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because it correctly maps Art. 131 but swaps Arts. 143 and 32, exploiting candidates who know Art. 32 is 'original' but forget it is original FRs jurisdiction, not advisory.
elimination_logic: Art. 131 is original jurisdiction for inter-governmental disputes — 'between the Government of India and one or more States' fits List II entry 2.
Art. 143 is advisory jurisdiction — the President refers questions of law or fact for SC's opinion; fits List II entry 4.
Art. 32 is original jurisdiction for enforcement of fundamental rights — distinct from Art. 131; fits List II entry 1.
Art. 129 declares SC a court of record empowering it to punish for contempt — fits List II entry 3; correct matching is A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in pairing Art. 32 and Art. 131. Both are 'original jurisdictions' of the SC, making students swap them. Art. 131 is original jurisdiction for Centre-State and inter-State disputes; Art. 32 is original jurisdiction for fundamental rights enforcement by any citizen. Placing 'FRs enforcement' under Art. 131 (or 'inter-governmental disputes' under Art. 32) is the classic conflation this question exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
The Supreme Court exercises several types of jurisdiction, each sourced from a distinct article.

Correct pairings:
• A-2: Art. 131 → Original jurisdiction for disputes between the Government of India and one or more States or between States inter se.
• B-4: Art. 143 → Advisory jurisdiction; President may refer questions of law or public importance to the SC for its opinion.
• C-1: Art. 32 → Original jurisdiction for enforcement of fundamental rights through appropriate writs; Art. 32 itself is a fundamental right.
• D-3: Art. 129 → Court of record; empowers SC to punish for contempt of itself.

Trap pairing: A and C (Arts. 131 and 32) are both 'original' jurisdictions; candidates frequently conflate them. Art. 131 is exclusively for governmental party disputes; Art. 32 is for any citizen enforcing FRs.

Value Addition:
• Art. 32 cannot be suspended during emergency under Art. 359 for rights under Arts. 20 and 21.
• Art. 143 opinions are advisory — not binding — though they carry great persuasive authority.
• Art. 129 court-of-record power coexists with appellate jurisdiction; they serve different purposes.

solution.concept_anchor: HC certificate refusal does not bar SLP under Art. 136
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because students reason that if HC refused the certificate, the party has exhausted HC remedies and cannot approach SC — forgetting that Art. 136 is a parallel, not sequential, track.
elimination_logic: The blank asks what recourse remains after HC refuses a certificate under Arts. 132/133/134.
Option (a) suggests no further recourse — this is incorrect; Art. 136 provides an independent pathway.
Option (c) suggests filing a fresh suit in DC — this conflates review of a judgment with original suits.
Option (d) suggests a writ under Art. 32 — Art. 32 is for FRs enforcement, not a substitute for appeal.
The correct option is (b): the party can approach the SC directly by filing an SLP under Art. 136.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Candidates who view the HC certificate as the exclusive gateway to SC appellate jurisdiction assume that refusal permanently bars further challenge. The key insight is that Arts. 132/133/134 and Art. 136 are parallel tracks, not sequential steps. Art. 136's SLP is an independent remedy that the SC may entertain regardless of what the HC decided about granting or refusing a certificate.
solution.final_explanation:
A High Court's refusal to grant a certificate of fitness under Articles 132, 133, or 134 does not permanently foreclose a party's access to the Supreme Court.

• Option (a): Incorrect — HC certificate refusal does not extinguish SC's jurisdiction; Art. 136 provides an independent route.
• Option (b): Correct — The party may file a Special Leave Petition directly before the Supreme Court under Art. 136. The SC independently evaluates whether to grant leave; it is not bound by the HC's refusal.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Filing a fresh suit in the District Court is a wholly different proceeding; it cannot undo or bypass the HC judgment under challenge.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Art. 32 is for fundamental rights enforcement; it cannot serve as a substitute for an appeal against an HC judgment where no independent FRs violation exists.

Value Addition:
• Arts. 132–134 and Art. 136 are parallel tracks — exhausting the certificate route is not a prerequisite for Art. 136.
• The SC can also examine whether an HC certificate was incorrectly granted or incorrectly refused.
• This dual-track design ensures that no litigant is left without recourse merely because the HC declined to certify fitness.

concepts_used: Review Jurisdiction under Article 137 as a Complement to Appellate Jurisdiction

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 137 review — no re-hearing, chambers, specific grounds

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 137, the Supreme Court can review any judgment or order made by itself, and such review proceedings involve a full re-hearing of the case with oral arguments from all parties.
statement_analysis.reason: Review under Art. 137 is typically decided in chambers without oral arguments; it is not a re-hearing of the case. Only in exceptional cases has oral argument been permitted.

statement_analysis.statement: The grounds for review under Article 137 are entirely left to the discretion of the Supreme Court and are not specified by any rule or parliamentary enactment.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 137 itself states that review is 'subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament or any rules made under Article 145'. SC Rules (Order XL) specify the grounds: error apparent on the face of record, new and important matter discovered, or any other sufficient reason.

statement_analysis.statement: A review petition under Article 137 must be filed before the same bench that delivered the original judgment.
statement_analysis.reason: The SC's practice and rules require that review petitions are placed before the same bench that decided the original matter — unless that is not possible, in which case a bench of equal strength is constituted.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Statement 2 only is incorrect) is a strong distractor because Statement 2's error about 'no grounds specified' is the most visible flaw; candidates may accept Statement 1 as correct under the assumption that 'review' means a full hearing.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1 — review under Art. 137 is decided in chambers without oral arguments (not a full re-hearing); Statement 1 is incorrect.

Test Statement 2 — grounds for review are specified in SC Rules under Art. 145 and any parliamentary law; the claim that grounds are 'entirely discretionary and unspecified' is incorrect; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Test Statement 3 — review is placed before the same bench that decided the original matter; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are both incorrect — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the intuition that 'review' means a fresh hearing. In judicial practice, review under Art. 137 is a constrained remedy — no fresh evidence, no oral arguments, decided in chambers on narrow grounds. This is precisely why the curative petition was evolved as a further remedy for genuine injustice. Candidates with only textbook knowledge accept Statement 1's description because it sounds procedurally complete.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 137 grants the SC power to review its own judgments — a narrow but important internal check on judicial errors.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Review proceedings under Art. 137 are held in chambers, typically without oral arguments. They are not re-hearings of the case. This contrasts with appellate hearings where full oral arguments are heard.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Art. 137 is 'subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament or any rules made under Article 145.' SC Rules (Order XL) specify three grounds: (i) error apparent on the face of the record, (ii) discovery of new and important matter, (iii) any other sufficient reason — the grounds are not left to pure discretion.
• Statement 3 — Correct: SC practice requires review petitions to be placed before the same bench that delivered the original judgment.

Value Addition:
• If review is dismissed, the curative petition (Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002) is the last resort — heard by three senior-most judges + original bench members.
• 'Error apparent on the face of the record' means an obvious, self-evident error that does not require elaborate examination to detect.
• Review cannot be used to introduce new arguments not raised in the original proceedings.

solution.concept_anchor: Art. 139A transfer — pending cases, not post-decision appeals
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Art. 136 SLP) is a strong distractor because students associate SC intervention in multiple litigation with the SLP power, not recognising that Art. 136 requires a decision to have been made, while Art. 139A targets pending cases.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves multiple identical tax cases PENDING before several HCs — no HC has yet decided them; this is not a post-decision situation.
Art. 136 SLP requires an existing judgment/order to challenge — eliminate option (b).
Art. 131 covers government v. government disputes — this is a citizen-vs-state tax matter; eliminate option (c).
Art. 143 is the presidential advisory reference — not relevant to pending litigation; eliminate option (d).
Art. 139A is designed exactly for this scenario: identical questions pending before multiple courts, transferred to SC or one HC for a uniform ruling — option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the tendency to associate SC intervention with Art. 136 SLP in all multi-court scenarios. Art. 136 requires an existing decision — it cannot be used for pending cases. Art. 139A is the constitutionally prescribed mechanism for consolidating pending cases with substantially similar questions of law, preventing conflicting HC rulings before they even arise. This is a pre-decision, preventive jurisdiction — a fundamental distinction.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 139A was designed to prevent conflicting rulings from multiple HCs on the same question of law by enabling pre-decision consolidation.

Applicable principle: Art. 139A empowers the SC to transfer cases involving the same or substantially similar questions of law pending before two or more HCs, or between an HC and the SC, to itself or to one HC for a uniform ruling.

Mapping to scenario: The identical income-tax deductibility question is pending (undecided) before five HCs. Art. 139A directly targets this situation — the SC can suo motu or on application transfer all these cases to itself.

• Option (a): Correct — Art. 139A is the precise provision for transferring pending cases with substantially similar questions.
• Option (b): Incorrect — Art. 136 SLP requires an existing judgment or order; pending cases cannot be the subject of an SLP.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Art. 131 is for disputes to which the Government of India and one or more States are parties; private taxpayer litigation is outside its scope.
• Option (d): Incorrect — Art. 143 is the President's advisory reference power; it is not available for pending private litigation.

Value Addition:
• Art. 139A was inserted by the 44th Amendment, 1978 — not an original provision.
• Transfer under Art. 139A can be suo motu or initiated by any party.
• Once transferred to SC, the HC's jurisdiction on those transferred cases is suspended.

solution.concept_anchor: Comparative features across Arts. 132/133/134/136

statement_analysis.statement: Article 132 is the only appellate provision that allows the Supreme Court to hear appeals from High Court decisions in criminal matters involving a constitutional question.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 133 covers only civil; Art. 134 covers criminal but NOT on constitutional grounds per se (it has its own conditions). Art. 132 uniquely covers criminal proceedings when a substantial constitutional question is involved.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 133, the High Court's certification requirement can be waived by the Supreme Court if the constitutional question is of exceptional national importance.
statement_analysis.reason: No provision in Art. 133 permits the SC to waive the HC certificate requirement; the HC certificate is mandatory under Art. 133. The only route without the HC certificate is Art. 136 SLP filed directly before the SC.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 136 has a wider coverage than Article 134 in that it can entertain appeals from any court or tribunal in India (excluding military courts), not just High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Art. 134 is strictly an HC-to-SC criminal track; Art. 136 covers any court or tribunal — Sessions Courts, NCLT, CAT, NGT, etc. — making its coverage far broader.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 134, the Supreme Court can hear a criminal appeal as of right (without certificate) when the High Court has awarded the death sentence irrespective of how the case reached the High Court.
statement_analysis.reason: The automatic right under Art. 134(1)(a)/(b) is conditioned on specific scenarios — HC reversing acquittal to death, or HC withdrawing and convicting with death. It is NOT available for every HC death sentence.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (only three correct) is a strong distractor for candidates who accept Statements 1, 2, and 3 while rejecting only Statement 4 because Statement 4's death-sentence trap is the most visible error.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Art. 132 uniquely covers criminal proceedings on constitutional grounds; correct.
Statement 2 — HC certificate under Art. 133 cannot be waived by SC; parties must go to Art. 136 SLP instead; incorrect.
Statement 3 — Art. 136 covers any court/tribunal vs. Art. 134's HC-only track; correct.
Statement 4 — automatic appeal under Art. 134 is scenario-specific, not triggered by every HC death sentence; incorrect. Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a plausible-fabrication trap — it sounds like a reasonable judicial flexibility but no such waiver power exists in Art. 133. Statement 4 is the classic death-sentence scope-extension trap: inflating the automatic jurisdiction to cover all death sentences. Together they test precision knowledge of conditions and limits across four constitutional provisions.
solution.final_explanation:
This question requires comparative knowledge of Arts. 132, 133, 134, and 136.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Art. 132 covers all three proceeding types (civil/criminal/other) on constitutional grounds. For a criminal proceeding involving a constitutional question, Art. 132 is the correct route.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: HC certificate under Art. 133 is mandatory; SC has no power to waive it. A party can bypass the certificate requirement only by going to Art. 136 SLP directly.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Art. 134 is an HC-to-SC criminal track only. Art. 136 sweeps much wider — any court or tribunal in India, except military courts-martial.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The automatic right under Art. 134 is not triggered by every HC death sentence. Only two scenarios qualify: (a) HC reversal of acquittal + death, and (b) HC withdrawal of case + conviction + death.

Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (b).

Value Addition:
• Art. 132 and Art. 134 may both apply to the same criminal case if it involves both a constitutional question AND a death sentence scenario.
• The SC (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 expanded Art. 134's reach via Parliament's Art. 134(2) power.
• SLP under Art. 136 is the residual 'catch-all' — it ensures no party is left without recourse.
